all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: immersive experience
concepts.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

defining_facts.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: virtual tour
concepts.definition: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

defining_facts.text: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually.

Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.

concepts.name: interaction
concepts.definition: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
Interaction in non-immersive settings, such as augmented reality (AR), is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture.

For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence.

Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: presence
concepts.definition: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

defining_facts.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.
Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.
The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: simulator sickness questionnaire
concepts.definition: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).

defining_facts.text: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).
The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) contains 16 items divided into three subscales: the oculomotor subscale, the disorientation subscale, and the nausea subscale.

In the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), participants rate the intensity of individual symptoms belonging to the oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales on a scale from 0 to 3, where a higher score denotes more severe symptoms.
The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) was not originally designed for virtual reality (VR) but was adapted for use in the context of virtual reality.
The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is the most extensively used of the questionnaires specifically designed for cyber sickness in extended reality (XR).

The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) was used to measure cyber sickness, and it is a standard questionnaire that is popular for measuring cyber sickness in immersive experiences although it was not originally developed for cyber sickness.
Participants rated their cyber sickness symptoms on the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) using a scale from 0 to 3, where 0 means no symptoms and 3 means the most severe symptoms.
The scores considered from the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) were nausea, disorientation, oculomotor discomfort, and total sickness.

The participants' simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) scores were computed before and after exposure and compared to get an idea of the effect of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour assessment design on those scores.

concepts.name: graphics processing unit
concepts.definition: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

defining_facts.text: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).
A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the hardware component that is used for speeding up the rendering process.

In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory.

An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering.

A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features.

A GPU is typically a multicore system in which many cores, each capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, work simultaneously on one single instruction and produce data simultaneously, and groups of cores form streaming multiprocessor units, each containing several cores.

A GPU is broadly organized with a host, input assemblers and a thread execution manager, where the manager allocates work to many streaming multiprocessors, each of which has a parallel data cache, and a texture storage stores predefined surface colors, with the elements exchanging data with global memory through load and store information.

The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience.

Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input.
Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.
The GPU computes vertex color by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.

The GPU projection stage combines viewing transformation, projection transformation and viewport transformation in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates, a continuous coordinate space, ready to be converted to pixels.

In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.
In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities that take place are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

In the pixel processing stage, the simplest surface texturing method applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point; GPUs store textures in high-speed texture storage on the graphics card, which each pixel calculation must access, and because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations, specialized memory caches reduce access time.

concepts.name: vision
concepts.definition: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

defining_facts.text: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

concepts.name: user categories
concepts.definition: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

defining_facts.text: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

concepts.name: questionnaire
concepts.definition: In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.

defining_facts.text: In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.
One major concern in user evaluation is that identifying suitable questionnaires is challenging.

In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session.

Well-known questionnaires available for post-task data collection include the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), designed by Lewis in 1991, and the Expectation Measure (EM), designed by Albert and Dixon in 2003.

Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

concepts.name: controlled experiment
concepts.definition: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

defining_facts.text: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in the context of usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

concepts.name: statistically significant difference
concepts.definition: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

defining_facts.text: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

In comparing two text-entry interfaces, a higher mean text-entry speed alone may be due to chance, so a statistically significant difference between the means is required to conclude that one design is better in speed or efficiency.

never_defined.name: hardware
never_defined.definition: The hardware market in the extended reality market is about 60 percent of the market size, and the software market is about 40 percent.

never_defined.name: software
never_defined.definition: The hardware market in the extended reality market is about 60 percent of the market size, and the software market is about 40 percent.

never_defined.name: virtual environment
never_defined.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

never_defined.name: nausea
never_defined.definition: A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.

never_defined.name: disorientation
never_defined.definition: A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.

never_defined.name: display resolution
never_defined.definition: Display resolution is a hardware factor that reduces cybersickness (CS) up to a certain point; a study evaluating 1K, 2K, 3K, and 4K resolutions found a substantial reduction in CS induction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K.

never_defined.name: rating scale
never_defined.definition: The outputs of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness (CS) are generally scores or ratings on rating scales, and these scores or ratings can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: exposure
never_defined.definition: To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky.

never_defined.name: controller-based interaction
never_defined.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

never_defined.name: personal computer
never_defined.definition: The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.

never_defined.name: virtual reality experience
never_defined.definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is used to speed up the rendering process because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process, and it is therefore very useful for rendering complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

never_defined.name: operating system
never_defined.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

never_defined.name: evaluation
never_defined.definition: The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.

never_defined.name: digital avatar
never_defined.definition: Creating digital avatars of the elements and objects of a physical space can preserve fragile artifacts that may not survive the passage of time.

never_defined.name: Majuli virtual reality tour
never_defined.definition: Usability requirements for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour were gathered by making field trips to Majuli, interviewing people, observing people in their natural work settings, and collecting data in the form of notes.

never_defined.name: research question
never_defined.definition: An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

never_defined.name: objective data
never_defined.definition: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

never_defined.name: prior-experience bias
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) experiment, unfamiliar users may produce results much different from familiar users, so a brief pre-experiment training session that demonstrates the system's features and how to use them can bring participants to the same level and reduce or nullify familiarity or prior-experience bias, which otherwise may lead to incorrect conclusions.
